clinicalPearls: Insulin-requiring diabetes appears in early infancy but remits, usually within the first months of life, distinguishing it clinically from the permanent forms.
The commonest cause is overexpression of the imprinted 6q24 locus (PLAGL1/ZAC and HYMAI), through paternal uniparental disomy, paternal duplication, or loss of maternal methylation.
Remission is not cure: a substantial proportion relapse with diabetes later in childhood or around puberty, so lifelong follow-up is essential.
Macroglossia and umbilical hernia are recognised clues in 6q24-related disease and help separate it from other neonatal diabetes.
Potassium-channel mutations (KCNJ11, ABCC8) can also produce a transient course, and these cases may respond to sulfonylureas at presentation and relapse.
Marked intrauterine growth restriction reflects deficient foetal insulin, mirroring the permanent forms.
A generalised imprinting disturbance (for example ZFP57-related) can accompany maternal hypomethylation and cause additional features.
reference.pathophysiology: Transient neonatal diabetes is dominated by disturbance of an imprinted region on chromosome 6q24 that normally shows monoallelic paternal expression. Excess dosage of the transcription factor PLAGL1 (ZAC) together with HYMAI, arising from paternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 6, paternal duplication of the 6q24 segment, or loss of methylation on the maternal allele, impairs the developmental regulation of insulin secretion during a critical perinatal window. Insulin deficiency during this period causes hyperglycaemia and poor growth, but as beta-cell regulation matures the requirement for exogenous insulin falls and diabetes remits. Because the underlying epigenetic or dosage lesion persists, beta-cell reserve remains vulnerable, and physiological stress or the insulin resistance of puberty can precipitate relapse. A minority of cases instead reflect activating potassium-channel mutations that transiently impair insulin release. Maternal hypomethylation may extend beyond 6q24 to other imprinted loci, producing a multilocus imprinting disturbance with a broader phenotype.
additionalDifferentials: Permanent neonatal diabetes mellitus (non-remitting monogenic disease)

additionalInvestigations: Methylation-specific analysis of the 6q24 differentially methylated region
Testing for paternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 6 and 6q24 duplication
Sequencing of KCNJ11 and ABCC8 to identify transient channel forms
Serum C-peptide with paired glucose to gauge residual beta-cell function
Islet autoantibody panel to exclude autoimmune diabetes
Serial glucose monitoring through remission and structured follow-up for relapse
redFlags: Dehydration or ketoacidosis at initial presentation despite the usually milder course
Failure to thrive with persistent hyperglycaemia in early infancy
Return of hyperglycaemic symptoms in later childhood or adolescence indicating relapse
Features suggesting a wider imprinting disorder beyond isolated diabetes
reference.prognosis: Neonatal diabetes typically remits within the first year with good short-term outcomes, but relapse later in childhood or at puberty is common and may require renewed treatment. Long-term prognosis is favourable when relapse is anticipated and managed, though lifelong metabolic surveillance is warranted.
pitfalls: Regarding remission as permanent cure and discharging the child from follow-up.
Failing to counsel families that diabetes frequently returns around puberty.
Not distinguishing 6q24 disease from potassium-channel forms, which alters treatment options.
Attributing macroglossia and umbilical hernia to an unrelated overgrowth syndrome.
Assuming a benign transient course means genetic confirmation is unnecessary.
references: International consensus guidance on monogenic and neonatal diabetes
Clinical genetics reference resources on imprinting disorders
management: Insulin replacement during the hyperglycaemic phase by continuous subcutaneous or intravenous insulin infusion, titrated to glycaemia and weaned as beta-cell function matures and diabetes remits
Trial of an oral sulfonylurea where a KCNJ11 or ABCC8 potassium-channel mutation is identified, as these transient forms may respond and permit insulin withdrawal
Optimise nutrition to correct the intrauterine growth restriction, with careful fluid and electrolyte balance in the neonatal period
Confirm the molecular basis (6q24 methylation defect, paternal uniparental disomy or duplication, or a channel gene) and involve clinical genetics with family counselling
Continuous glucose monitoring through remission, with C-peptide and paired glucose to gauge residual beta-cell reserve
Lifelong metabolic surveillance because remission is not cure, anticipating relapse in later childhood and around puberty
Reintroduce glucose-lowering therapy promptly at relapse and involve paediatric endocrinology
